scenes.title: Live Demo 2: Phone UI & Physical Button Advancement
Live Demo 3: Remote Scenario Execution & Emergency Stop
Live Demo 4: Wireless Keyboard & Multi-Touch Trackpad Mouse
Live Demo 5: Adversarial Evasion & Cadence Jitter
Live Demo 6: WHID-Guard Host Defense in Action

subtitles.text: Hello everyone, and welcome to the live demonstration of our cybersecurity project: WHID-Guard, an ESP32-S3 Phone-Controlled USB HID Keyboard and Mouse platform with BadUSB Simulation and a Defensive Keystroke Firewall.
Developed by Ram Karthik G and Harini V from the Department of Cybersecurity at Amrita Vishwa Vidyapeetham, Chennai.

In this video, we will show you the physical hardware setup, live automated keystroke injection, wireless smartphone remote control, and our real-time behavioral host firewall actively defending against the attack.
Let's begin with the live hardware demonstration.
On the left, you see our Windows laptop desktop.
When the ESP32-S3 is plugged in, its native USB-OTG controller on GPIO 19 and 20 enumerates instantly as a standard USB HID composite device without requiring any third-party drivers.
Watch the screen closely: after a bounded 3.5-second stabilization wait, the ESP32 triggers Scenario 1.
It automatically opens the Windows Run dialog, types notepad, and launches the editor.
Notice how the microcontroller types our security awareness advisory character-by-character at high speed without anyone touching the laptop keyboard.
Now look at the right pane, where our real smartphone controller is connected to the ESP32-S3 over Wi-Fi.
The phone browser loads our dark-mode Single-Page Application served directly from the microcontroller's flash memory.
In the Settings tab, we enter the security PIN and authenticate against the REST API.
The top telemetry immediately confirms our session token.

Next, watch what happens when I press the physical GPIO 0 BOOT button on the ESP32 board: the hardware edge-detector advances circularly through our payload sequences, cycling from Scenario 1 to 2, 3, and 4 with a 50-millisecond debounce filter.
From the phone's Scenarios tab, we can also launch any attack directly.
Watch as I tap Scenario 4 on the phone.
On the laptop, the Run dialog opens instantly, launches the Command Prompt, and runs netsh wlan show profiles, non-destructively enumerating all saved wireless networks.
Next, I trigger Scenario 3: simulated ransomware.
But watch this safety feature: while it is typing, I immediately tap the red Emergency Stop button on the phone!
The firmware's non-blocking loop halts typing within 10 milliseconds and calls releaseAll on both keyboard and mouse buses, leaving zero keys stuck.
Beyond security payloads, the platform converts the smartphone into a complete driverless input peripheral.
In the Keyboard tab, we have a full 6-row desktop keyboard with persistent hardware modifier latches, system shortcut macros, and a live text transmitter.
On the laptop, I open a text file and type directly from the phone.
Switching to the Mouse tab gives us a 60-hertz virtual trackpad.
Moving a finger across the phone screen smoothly translates into 8-bit cursor movement on the laptop, supporting tap-to-click, drag-lock, and precision nudging.
Standard BadUSB tools type with robotic consistency, making them easy to catch with naive speed thresholds.
In this demonstration, we test our firmware's Adversarial Stealth Mode.
On the phone, I toggle the Adversarial Evasion switch.

Notice how the typing cadence transforms: the firmware replaces rigid 10-millisecond delays with randomized stochastic jitter, and inserts cognitive pauses of 150 to 300 milliseconds after spaces and punctuation.
This emulates authentic human thinking pauses, designed to stress-test host defensive classifiers.
Now, let's observe our defensive solution: WHID-Guard.
On the laptop, we launch our Python Keystroke Firewall.
Look at the live telemetry card: using the Windows Raw Input API, it immediately attributes the active device handle to the ESP32-S3 with Vendor ID 303A.
I click Toggle to arm the firewall.
Now, I trigger a BadUSB payload from the phone.
Watch the firewall: within just 8 characters—less than 85 milliseconds—the keystroke dynamics engine detects the near-zero variance, trips the anomaly threshold, and locks down the device!
As you can see, zero characters reach Notepad.
And most importantly, when I type on the laptop's built-in keyboard, it types perfectly!
Only the malicious hardware handle is quarantined.
We benchmarked WHID-Guard across 1,500 keystrokes.
In human baseline testing, the system achieved a 0.0 percent False Positive Rate across 500 consecutive keystrokes.
Against unconstrained BadUSB injection, it achieved a 98.6 percent True Positive Rate, quarantining the attack within 8 characters or 85 milliseconds.
Against adversarial evasion, it flagged 25.2 percent of suspicious events.
In conclusion, WHID-Guard successfully demonstrates the threat of hardware implants while introducing a practical, per-device behavioral defense.
Our complete IEEE research paper and open-source codebase are available on GitHub.
Thank you for your time and evaluation.
